newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: EU summit on track for last-ditch treaty deal.
newsitem.headline: EU summit on track for last-ditch treaty deal.

text.p: European Union leaders pieced together some of the key elements of a package of reforms on Tuesday, indicating they could finalise a new treaty as talks at a two-day summit went down to the wire.

After the near-euphoria of brokering a Franco-German peace on monetary union on Monday, leaders painstakingly sifted through individual member state objections to parts of a draft text in a bid to fine-tune a revised treaty.

With 15 months of low-profile negotiation behind them, leaders were intent to reach agreement at Amsterdam in order to send a positive signal to up to a dozen eastern European countries queuing to join the wealthy western club.
Much of the likely new treaty is aimed at streamlining the 15-member bloc to accommodate new partners and avoid paralysis in the joint decision-making process.
The long treaty negotiations leading up to the summit had already toned down much of what the bloc had hoped to achieve in terms of signalling a new Citizens' Europe for the next century.
Having promised aspirant members that accession talks could open six months after agreeing a new treaty, the EU was eager not to let the negotiations drag on.
Asked whether it would be damaging if leaders failed to agree on Tuesday, European External Relations Commissioner Hans van den Broek said: "It would certainly be a big blow.

"I still think there is the political will to reach an agreement tonight, but if it isn't tonight, it must be some other night...one thing's for certain, the status quo can't endure. The road is still slippery."
Member states looked set to continue the eleventh-hour haggling and protecting their own national interests on key areas late into the night.
There were some successes, however.

British Prime Minister Tony Blair claimed victory for a deal on defence policy, effectively postponing the question of whether Europe's 10-nation Western European Union (WEU) defence arm should be merged into the bloc.

After hours of negotiation, the leaders agreed to a form of words appeasing London and the bloc's neutral countries and calling for the EU to develop closer relations with the WEU, with an eye to the "possibility" of an eventual merger.
A Franco-german led group had wanted to fully integrate the WEU into the Union to build a European defence architecture alongside the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation.
But Britain, backed for different reasons by Denmark, Sweden, Finland, Austria and Ireland, warned this could undermine NATO's position as Europe's security bedrock.

The summit still faced tough negotiations on perhaps the trickiest issues -- power sharing among EU members and flexibility, where a majority of countries want to retain a veto to prevent them from being left behind by eager integrationists.

The larger states, like France, have insisted on more clout in decision-making to make up for an erosion of their power-base as more countries have joined the bloc. But their smaller partners have railed against the plan.

Grand designs to appoint a senior figure to give a single face and voice to a credible common European foreign and security policy have, however, come to little, with the 15 leaders appearing set to give a little-known Eurocrat the job of representing the Union in foreign policy.

Under revised drafts, EU countries would agree to cooperate more closely on asylum, immigration, visa policy and crime fighting, although island states Britain and Ireland would be given an opt-out, as would Denmark.

The move to beef up cooperation on borders and immigration is part of the EU's plans to create an area of freedom, security and justice designed to appeal to citizens who are turning away from the bloc because of austerity programmes needed to get monetary union off its planned January 1999 launch-pad.
Anticipating lengthy negotiations, German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel insisted: "The European train remains on track and keeps on puffing."
